Switchbox maintains three versions of NREL's ResStock dataset for Maryland: the raw
NREL release, a Switchbox-processed `_sb` release (utility assignment, heating-type
classification, metadata enrichment), and an ACH-ratio infiltration-corrected
`_sb_ach_ratio` release (a fitted-ratio ACH50 correction — see
[`resstock_ach.qmd`](resstock_ach.qmd)'s "Fitted-ratio correction" section — and the
release the current MD BGE batch actually runs CAIRO against; see
`rate-design-platform/rate_design/hp_rates/md/config/scenarios/pipeline_bge.yaml`).
[`investigation_er_hp_loads.md`](investigation_er_hp_loads.md) first flagged that the
electric-resistance (ER) → heat-pump (HP) load-change picture shifts across these three
releases. This notebook quantifies that shift at the **per-building level** for BGE's
electric-heating homes: the delta in total annual electric consumption between upgrade 00
and upgrade 01, the same delta restricted to the winter heating season (October–March,
both as a single whole-winter number and broken out month by month), and both of those
repeated for electric *heating input* only (rather than total electric, which also
includes cooling and everything else).

The bulk of the notebook covers the **electric-resistance (ER)** homes that upgrade 01
converts to a heat pump. The monthly percent-change section at the end repeats the two
key charts for three populations: ER homes, homes that **already have a heat pump** at
baseline, and the two **combined** — the last being the population that matches
whole-home billing data which identifies electric-heating customers without
distinguishing strip heat from heat pumps.

Throughout, **delta = upgrade 01 − upgrade 00**, so a negative delta means the HP upgrade
*reduces* electric consumption relative to the ER baseline.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import plotnine as p9
import polars as pl

from lib.plotnine import SB_COLORS, theme_switchbox
from lib.quarto import display_figure
from lib.rates_analysis.ncp_funcs import grid_consumption_expr
from lib.rates_analysis.rate_case_funcs import (
    plot_weighted_hist_by_group,
    weighted_mean,
    weighted_pct,
    weighted_quantile,
)
```

## Parameters

We compare three releases, keyed by their directory suffix under
`/ebs/data/nrel/resstock/`. Each entry's `label` is what shows up in every table and
chart in this notebook, in this same left-to-right/top-to-bottom order.

```{python}
#| label: params-releases

STATE = "MD"
UTILITY = "bge"
EBS_BASE = Path("/ebs/data/nrel/resstock")

RELEASES = {
    "raw": {"path": EBS_BASE / "res_2024_amy2018_2", "label": "Raw NREL"},
    "sb": {"path": EBS_BASE / "res_2024_amy2018_2_sb", "label": "Switchbox-processed"},
    "sb_ach_ratio": {"path": EBS_BASE / "res_2024_amy2018_2_sb_ach_ratio", "label": "ACH-ratio corrected"},
}
RELEASE_ORDER = [r["label"] for r in RELEASES.values()]
RELEASE_COLORS = {
    "Raw NREL": SB_COLORS["sky"],
    "Switchbox-processed": SB_COLORS["carrot"],
    "ACH-ratio corrected": SB_COLORS["midnight"],
}
```

Upgrade 00 is the ER baseline and upgrade 01 is NREL's "ENERGY STAR heat pump with
electric backup" upgrade — present in all three releases. Only the `_sb` and
`_sb_ach_ratio` releases carry ResStock's heating-type classification
(`postprocess_group.heating_type_v2`) and utility assignment
(`sb.electric_utility`); the raw release has neither. Since `bldg_id` identity is shared
across all three releases (they're the same underlying buildings, just with different
load-correction steps applied), we derive the BGE-electric-resistance population once
from `_sb` and reuse that same set of buildings — and the same ResStock sample
`weight`, which reflects sampling probability, not any load correction — across all
three releases. That's what makes the raw/`_sb`/`_sb_ach_ratio` numbers below directly
comparable at the per-building level.

```{python}
#| label: params-population

POPULATION_RELEASE = "sb"
UPGRADE_BASE = "00"
UPGRADE_HP = "01"

# Display labels for the three populations we chart, used in plot titles.
LABEL_ER = "BGE electric-resistance homes"
LABEL_HP = "BGE existing-heat-pump homes"
LABEL_COMBINED = "BGE electric-resistance + heat-pump homes"
```

The month-by-month breakdown covers the **full calendar year**, since the HP upgrade
changes cooling-season consumption too, not just heating. We keep a separate winter
definition (October through March) for the whole-heating-season aggregate. ResStock's
hourly load curves carry a `month` column (1–12), so we aggregate on that directly
rather than relying on a monthly load-curve file — the raw release doesn't have one for
MD, so hourly is the common denominator across all three releases.

```{python}
#| label: params-months

ALL_MONTHS = list(range(1, 13))
WINTER_MONTHS = [10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3]
MONTH_NUM_TO_LABEL = {
    1: "Jan",
    2: "Feb",
    3: "Mar",
    4: "Apr",
    5: "May",
    6: "Jun",
    7: "Jul",
    8: "Aug",
    9: "Sep",
    10: "Oct",
    11: "Nov",
    12: "Dec",
}
MONTH_ORDER = [MONTH_NUM_TO_LABEL[m] for m in ALL_MONTHS]
WINTER_MONTH_LABELS = [MONTH_NUM_TO_LABEL[m] for m in WINTER_MONTHS]
```

Electric heating input is the sum of ResStock's four heating-related electricity
end-uses (main heating, heating fans/pumps, and the heat pump's electric-resistance
backup coils, both steady-state and freeze-avoidance) — the same `HEATING_E_COLS`
convention used in `investigation_er_hp_loads.md` and `resstock_ach.qmd`. Annual load
curves suffix these columns with `.kwh`; hourly load curves don't.

```{python}
#| label: params-heating-cols

HEATING_E_COLS_ANNUAL = [
    "out.electricity.heating.energy_consumption.kwh",
    "out.electricity.heating_fans_pumps.energy_consumption.kwh",
    "out.electricity.heating_hp_bkup.energy_consumption.kwh",
    "out.electricity.heating_hp_bkup_fa.energy_consumption.kwh",
]
HEATING_E_COLS_HOURLY = [c.replace(".kwh", "") for c in HEATING_E_COLS_ANNUAL]
```

## Population: BGE electric-resistance and heat-pump homes

We load `_sb`'s upgrade-00 metadata and utility assignment once, then filter to two
disjoint BGE populations by baseline heating type
(`postprocess_group.heating_type_v2`) — ResStock's own classification, not a
re-derivation from raw fuel/equipment fields:

- **Electric resistance** (ER): homes whose baseline heating is electric resistance, so
  upgrade 01 is a genuine fuel-switch-in-place from strip heat to a heat pump.
- **Existing heat pump** (HP): homes that *already* have a heat pump at baseline, so
  upgrade 01 is an efficiency upgrade rather than an equipment-type change.
- **Combined**: the union of the two, which is the population BGE's own billing data
  would correspond to if it identifies electric-heating customers without
  distinguishing strip heat from heat pumps.

```{python}
#| label: load-population

pop_release_path = RELEASES[POPULATION_RELEASE]["path"]
meta = pl.read_parquet(
    pop_release_path / "metadata" / f"state={STATE}" / f"upgrade={UPGRADE_BASE}" / "metadata-sb.parquet"
)
ua = pl.read_parquet(pop_release_path / "metadata_utility" / f"state={STATE}" / "utility_assignment.parquet")
bge_ids = ua.filter(pl.col("sb.electric_utility") == UTILITY).select("bldg_id")


def bge_population_by_heating_type(heating_type: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """BGE bldg_id + weight for one `postprocess_group.heating_type_v2` value."""
    return (
        meta.join(bge_ids, on="bldg_id", how="semi")
        .filter(pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2") == heating_type)
        .select("bldg_id", "weight")
    )


population_er = bge_population_by_heating_type("electrical_resistance")
population_hp = bge_population_by_heating_type("heat_pump")
population_combined = pl.concat([population_er, population_hp], how="vertical")
```

The two heating types are mutually exclusive in `heating_type_v2`, so the combined
population is a straight concatenation with no building counted twice — worth asserting
rather than assuming, since double-counting would silently inflate every weighted
statistic downstream.

```{python}
#| label: show-population

assert population_combined["bldg_id"].n_unique() == population_combined.height, "ER and HP populations overlap"

for label, pop in [(LABEL_ER, population_er), (LABEL_HP, population_hp), (LABEL_COMBINED, population_combined)]:
    print(f"{label:45s} {pop.height:>6,d} buildings, {pop['weight'].sum():>10,.0f} weighted customers")
```

## Annual load, per release

Each release has a single per-state, per-upgrade annual load-curve file with one row
per building. We compute two per-building metrics from it: total grid consumption
(`max(total − |pv|, 0)`, matching CAIRO's billing basis via
`grid_consumption_expr()`) and electric heating input (the four `HEATING_E_COLS_ANNUAL`
summed).

```{python}
#| label: annual-loader


def load_annual_release(release_path: Path, upgrade: str, ids: list[int]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """One release/upgrade's annual total + heating electric kWh, for a fixed building set."""
    path = (
        release_path
        / "load_curve_annual"
        / f"state={STATE}"
        / f"upgrade={upgrade}"
        / f"{STATE}_upgrade{upgrade}_metadata_and_annual_results.parquet"
    )
    lf = pl.scan_parquet(path).filter(pl.col("bldg_id").is_in(ids))
    return lf.select(
        "bldg_id",
        grid_consumption_expr(
            load_col="out.electricity.total.energy_consumption.kwh",
            pv_col="out.electricity.pv.energy_consumption.kwh",
        ).alias("total_kwh"),
        sum((pl.col(c) for c in HEATING_E_COLS_ANNUAL), start=pl.lit(0.0)).alias("heating_kwh"),
    ).collect()
```

For each release, we load upgrade 00 and upgrade 01 separately, join them on
`bldg_id`, and take `delta = upg01 − upg00` for both metrics. `annual_delta_for_release`
takes a `population` (bldg_id + weight) so we can reuse it for the ER population here,
the heat-pump population below, and the combined population further down, without
duplicating the loading/joining logic.

```{python}
#| label: annual-delta-per-release


def annual_delta_for_release(key: str, population: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Per-building annual total/heating delta (upg01 - upg00) for one release."""
    ids = population["bldg_id"].to_list()
    release_path = RELEASES[key]["path"]
    upg0 = load_annual_release(release_path, UPGRADE_BASE, ids).rename(
        {"total_kwh": "total_kwh_upg0", "heating_kwh": "heating_kwh_upg0"}
    )
    upg1 = load_annual_release(release_path, UPGRADE_HP, ids).rename(
        {"total_kwh": "total_kwh_upg1", "heating_kwh": "heating_kwh_upg1"}
    )
    return (
        upg0.join(upg1, on="bldg_id")
        .join(population, on="bldg_id")
        .with_columns(
            (pl.col("total_kwh_upg1") - pl.col("total_kwh_upg0")).alias("delta_total"),
            (pl.col("heating_kwh_upg1") - pl.col("heating_kwh_upg0")).alias("delta_heating"),
        )
        .with_columns(pl.lit(RELEASES[key]["label"]).alias("release"))
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: annual-deltas-combine

annual_deltas_er = pl.concat(
    [annual_delta_for_release(k, population_er) for k in RELEASES], how="vertical"
).with_columns(pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)))
annual_deltas_er.head()
```

## Winter and monthly load, per release

Sub-annual figures come from per-building hourly files (`{bldg_id}-{upgrade}.parquet`).
We compute the same two per-hour metrics as above, then aggregate two ways: grouping by
`bldg_id` over the six winter months gives the whole-winter total; grouping by `bldg_id`
and `month` over all twelve months gives the individual-month totals.

```{python}
#| label: hourly-loader


def load_hourly_release(release_path: Path, upgrade: str, ids: list[int], months: list[int]) -> pl.LazyFrame:
    """Hourly total/heating grid consumption for a fixed building set and month set.

    Constructs per-building parquet paths directly rather than scanning the whole
    hourly partition and filtering, matching the "single utility from S3" guidance
    (avoids probing every file just to keep a handful of buildings' rows) -- even
    though these reads are local, it keeps the pattern consistent with
    lib.rates_analysis.ncp_funcs.scan_hourly_loads_for_buildings.
    """
    load_dir = release_path / "load_curve_hourly" / f"state={STATE}" / f"upgrade={upgrade}"
    upgrade_int = str(int(upgrade))
    paths = [str(load_dir / f"{bid}-{upgrade_int}.parquet") for bid in ids]
    return (
        pl.scan_parquet(paths)
        .filter(pl.col("month").is_in(months))
        .select(
            "bldg_id",
            "month",
            grid_consumption_expr().alias("total_kwh"),
            sum((pl.col(c) for c in HEATING_E_COLS_HOURLY), start=pl.lit(0.0)).alias("heating_kwh"),
        )
    )


def winter_totals_for_release(release_path: Path, upgrade: str, ids: list[int]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Whole-winter (Oct-Mar) total/heating kWh, one row per building."""
    return (
        load_hourly_release(release_path, upgrade, ids, WINTER_MONTHS)
        .group_by("bldg_id")
        .agg(pl.col("total_kwh").sum(), pl.col("heating_kwh").sum())
        .collect()
    )


def monthly_for_release(release_path: Path, upgrade: str, ids: list[int]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Per-calendar-month total/heating kWh, twelve rows per building."""
    return (
        load_hourly_release(release_path, upgrade, ids, ALL_MONTHS)
        .group_by("bldg_id", "month")
        .agg(pl.col("total_kwh").sum(), pl.col("heating_kwh").sum())
        .collect()
    )
```

Same upg01 − upg00 delta pattern as the annual section, once for the whole-winter
aggregate and once for the per-month breakdown.

```{python}
#| label: winter-delta-per-release


def winter_delta_for_release(key: str, population: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Per-building whole-winter total/heating delta (upg01 - upg00) for one release."""
    ids = population["bldg_id"].to_list()
    release_path = RELEASES[key]["path"]
    upg0 = winter_totals_for_release(release_path, UPGRADE_BASE, ids).rename(
        {"total_kwh": "total_kwh_upg0", "heating_kwh": "heating_kwh_upg0"}
    )
    upg1 = winter_totals_for_release(release_path, UPGRADE_HP, ids).rename(
        {"total_kwh": "total_kwh_upg1", "heating_kwh": "heating_kwh_upg1"}
    )
    return (
        upg0.join(upg1, on="bldg_id")
        .join(population, on="bldg_id")
        .with_columns(
            (pl.col("total_kwh_upg1") - pl.col("total_kwh_upg0")).alias("delta_total"),
            (pl.col("heating_kwh_upg1") - pl.col("heating_kwh_upg0")).alias("delta_heating"),
        )
        .with_columns(pl.lit(RELEASES[key]["label"]).alias("release"))
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: winter-deltas-combine

winter_deltas_er = pl.concat(
    [winter_delta_for_release(k, population_er) for k in RELEASES], how="vertical"
).with_columns(pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)))
winter_deltas_er.head()
```

```{python}
#| label: monthly-delta-per-release


def monthly_delta_for_release(key: str, population: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Per-building, per-calendar-month total/heating delta (upg01 - upg00) for one release."""
    ids = population["bldg_id"].to_list()
    release_path = RELEASES[key]["path"]
    upg0 = monthly_for_release(release_path, UPGRADE_BASE, ids).rename(
        {"total_kwh": "total_kwh_upg0", "heating_kwh": "heating_kwh_upg0"}
    )
    upg1 = monthly_for_release(release_path, UPGRADE_HP, ids).rename(
        {"total_kwh": "total_kwh_upg1", "heating_kwh": "heating_kwh_upg1"}
    )
    return (
        upg0.join(upg1, on=["bldg_id", "month"])
        .join(population, on="bldg_id")
        .with_columns(
            (pl.col("total_kwh_upg1") - pl.col("total_kwh_upg0")).alias("delta_total"),
            (pl.col("heating_kwh_upg1") - pl.col("heating_kwh_upg0")).alias("delta_heating"),
        )
        .with_columns(
            pl.lit(RELEASES[key]["label"]).alias("release"),
            pl.col("month").replace_strict(MONTH_NUM_TO_LABEL).alias("month_label"),
        )
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: monthly-deltas-combine

monthly_deltas_er = pl.concat(
    [monthly_delta_for_release(k, population_er) for k in RELEASES], how="vertical"
).with_columns(
    pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)),
    pl.col("month_label").cast(pl.Enum(MONTH_ORDER)),
)
monthly_deltas_er.head()
```

Let's run a quick sanity check: restricted to the six winter months, each building's
monthly deltas should sum to exactly its whole-winter delta, since both are derived from
the same underlying hourly rows just aggregated differently.

```{python}
#| label: sanity-check-monthly-sums-to-winter

_check = (
    monthly_deltas_er.filter(pl.col("month").is_in(WINTER_MONTHS))
    .group_by("bldg_id", "release")
    .agg(pl.col("delta_total").sum().alias("sum_of_monthly_deltas"))
    .join(winter_deltas_er.select("bldg_id", "release", "delta_total"), on=["bldg_id", "release"])
    .with_columns((pl.col("sum_of_monthly_deltas") - pl.col("delta_total")).abs().alias("diff"))
)
max_diff = _check["diff"].max()
print(f"Max |sum of monthly deltas - whole-winter delta|: {max_diff:.2e} kWh")
assert max_diff < 1e-6, "Monthly deltas don't sum to the whole-winter delta -- aggregation bug"
```

## Summary statistics

For each metric, we report the weighted mean delta, weighted median delta, and the
weighted percent of homes where the HP upgrade *increases* consumption (`delta > 0`),
one row per release.

```{python}
#| label: summarize-helper


def summarize_by_release(df: pl.DataFrame, value_col: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Weighted mean/median delta and % of homes with an increase, one row per release."""
    rows = [
        {
            "release": release,
            "mean_delta": weighted_mean(sub, value_col),
            "median_delta": weighted_quantile(sub, value_col, 0.5),
            "pct_increase": weighted_pct(sub, pl.col(value_col) > 0) * 100,
            "n_weighted": sub["weight"].sum(),
        }
        for release in RELEASE_ORDER
        if (sub := df.filter(pl.col("release") == release)).height > 0
    ]
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)
```

### Individual calendar months

Same three stats, but computed separately for each release/month combination.

```{python}
#| label: summarize-monthly-helper


def summarize_by_release_month(df: pl.DataFrame, value_col: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Weighted mean/median delta and % of homes with an increase, per release x month."""
    rows = [
        {
            "release": release,
            "month": month,
            "mean_delta": weighted_mean(sub, value_col),
            "median_delta": weighted_quantile(sub, value_col, 0.5),
            "pct_increase": weighted_pct(sub, pl.col(value_col) > 0) * 100,
        }
        for release in RELEASE_ORDER
        for month in MONTH_ORDER
        if (
            sub := df.filter((pl.col("release") == release) & (pl.col("month_label") == month))
        ).height
        > 0
    ]
    return pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(
        pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)),
        pl.col("month").cast(pl.Enum(MONTH_ORDER)),
    )
```

## Heat-pump and combined populations

Everything above covers the ER homes. Because the three delta helpers take a
`population` argument, we can run the identical pipeline over the existing-heat-pump
homes without duplicating any loading or joining logic.

```{python}
#| label: hp-deltas

annual_deltas_hp = pl.concat(
    [annual_delta_for_release(k, population_hp) for k in RELEASES], how="vertical"
).with_columns(pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)))
winter_deltas_hp = pl.concat(
    [winter_delta_for_release(k, population_hp) for k in RELEASES], how="vertical"
).with_columns(pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)))
monthly_deltas_hp = pl.concat(
    [monthly_delta_for_release(k, population_hp) for k in RELEASES], how="vertical"
).with_columns(
    pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)),
    pl.col("month_label").cast(pl.Enum(MONTH_ORDER)),
)
```

The combined population needs no new file reads. These frames are one row per building
(per month, in the monthly case) and the two populations are disjoint, so stacking them
gives exactly the frame we'd get by running the loaders over the union of building IDs.

```{python}
#| label: combined-deltas

annual_deltas_combined = pl.concat([annual_deltas_er, annual_deltas_hp], how="vertical")
winter_deltas_combined = pl.concat([winter_deltas_er, winter_deltas_hp], how="vertical")
monthly_deltas_combined = pl.concat([monthly_deltas_er, monthly_deltas_hp], how="vertical")
```

To compare populations side by side, we stack each population's `summarize_by_release`
output with a `population` column.

```{python}
#| label: cross-population-helper

ANNUAL_DELTAS = {LABEL_ER: annual_deltas_er, LABEL_HP: annual_deltas_hp, LABEL_COMBINED: annual_deltas_combined}
WINTER_DELTAS = {LABEL_ER: winter_deltas_er, LABEL_HP: winter_deltas_hp, LABEL_COMBINED: winter_deltas_combined}
MONTHLY_DELTAS = {
    LABEL_ER: monthly_deltas_er,
    LABEL_HP: monthly_deltas_hp,
    LABEL_COMBINED: monthly_deltas_combined,
}


def summarize_across_populations(frames: dict[str, pl.DataFrame], value_col: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """summarize_by_release run per population, stacked with a `population` column."""
    return pl.concat(
        [summarize_by_release(df, value_col).with_columns(pl.lit(label).alias("population")) for label, df in frames.items()],
        how="vertical",
    ).select("population", "release", "mean_delta", "median_delta", "pct_increase", "n_weighted")
```



```{python}
summarize_across_populations(WINTER_DELTAS, "delta_total")
```

## Monthly trend: percent change by month

The histograms above collapse each release's winter into one number, and the absolute
kWh deltas in the previous sections are hard to compare release to release, since the
ACH50 correction shifts each release's *baseline* load level too -- a bigger baseline
can produce a bigger absolute delta even if the HP upgrade has the same proportional
effect. So here we plot each release's delta as a **percent change relative to that
release's own upgrade-00 baseline**, month by month across the full calendar year. We use
a ratio of weighted sums (population-level kWh saved divided by population-level baseline
kWh) rather than a weighted mean of each building's own percent change, since a handful of
homes have near-zero baseline heating load in shoulder months -- dividing by a near-zero
baseline would blow up those buildings' individual percent changes into outliers.

```{python}
#| label: summarize-pct-change-helper


def summarize_pct_change_by_release_month(df: pl.DataFrame, delta_col: str, baseline_col: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Weighted % change (ratio of weighted sums), one row per release x month.

    A month with no weighted baseline load at all yields None rather than a divide-by-zero:
    it can't happen for the BGE populations here, but it would for a utility/state whose
    summer heating load rounds to nothing.
    """
    rows = []
    for release in RELEASE_ORDER:
        for month in MONTH_ORDER:
            sub = df.filter((pl.col("release") == release) & (pl.col("month_label") == month))
            if sub.height == 0:
                continue
            baseline = (sub[baseline_col] * sub["weight"]).sum()
            delta = (sub[delta_col] * sub["weight"]).sum()
            rows.append(
                {
                    "release": release,
                    "month": month,
                    "pct_delta": delta / baseline * 100 if baseline > 0 else None,
                }
            )
    return pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(
        pl.col("release").cast(pl.Enum(RELEASE_ORDER)),
        pl.col("month").cast(pl.Enum(MONTH_ORDER)),
    )
```

We compute two metrics -- whole-home total electric use, and electric heating input --
for each of the three populations, giving the six series we chart below.

One caveat on reading the heating charts in summer: heating is a rounding error in June
through September (under 1% of total electric use in those months), so the percent change
there is a ratio of two very small numbers. It's real, but it describes almost no kWh.

```{python}
#| label: monthly-pct-change-summary

monthly_total_pct = {
    label: summarize_pct_change_by_release_month(df, "delta_total", "total_kwh_upg0")
    for label, df in MONTHLY_DELTAS.items()
}
monthly_heating_pct = {
    label: summarize_pct_change_by_release_month(df, "delta_heating", "heating_kwh_upg0")
    for label, df in MONTHLY_DELTAS.items()
}
```

```{python}
#| label: monthly-pct-change-table

pl.concat(
    [df.with_columns(pl.lit(label).alias("population")) for label, df in monthly_total_pct.items()],
    how="vertical",
).pivot(on="release", index=["population", "month"], values="pct_delta")
```

Each chart shows one line per release, so the vertical spread between lines is the
release effect and the shape across months is the seasonal effect.

```{python}
#| label: pct-change-plot-helper


def pct_axis_labels(breaks: list[float]) -> list[str]:
    """Percent labels, adding a decimal only when the chosen breaks need one.

    The HP population's total-electric range is narrow enough that matplotlib picks
    2.5-point steps; formatting those with no decimals would print -2% for -2.5%.
    """
    decimals = 0 if all(float(b).is_integer() for b in breaks if b == b) else 1
    return [f"{b:.{decimals}f}%" for b in breaks]


def plot_monthly_pct_change(summary: pl.DataFrame, metric_label: str, population_label: str) -> p9.ggplot:
    """Weighted % change by calendar month, one line per release."""
    return (
        p9.ggplot(summary, p9.aes(x="month", y="pct_delta", color="release", group="release"))
        + p9.geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dotted", color="gray")
        + p9.geom_line(size=1)
        + p9.geom_point(size=2.5)
        + p9.scale_color_manual(values=RELEASE_COLORS, breaks=RELEASE_ORDER)
        + p9.scale_y_continuous(labels=pct_axis_labels)
        + p9.labs(
            x="Month",
            y="Weighted % change (upg01 vs upg00)",
            color="Release",
            title=f"{population_label}: % change in {metric_label}",
        )
        + theme_switchbox()
        + p9.theme(figure_size=(10.5, 4.5))
    )
```

Across all three populations, the heating-input percent change moves very little
between releases, while the total-electric percent change moves more. That asymmetry
follows from what the ACH50 correction actually rescales: electric heating and electric
cooling, but *not* the remaining end uses (lighting, appliances, plug loads, water
heating). In the heating charts, both the numerator and the denominator of the ratio are
made up entirely of rescaled quantities, so the correction largely cancels out. In the
total-electric charts, the denominator also contains untouched non-space-conditioning
load, which dilutes the correction differently in each release and leaves a visible gap
between the lines.

## Monthly trend: absolute kWh

The percent-change charts above cancel out each release's baseline so the *proportional*
effect of upgrade 01 is comparable. The charts below keep the units in kWh: weighted
mean of the per-building delta (upgrade 01 − upgrade 00), one line per release. Negative
values are savings. This is where the ACH50 correction shows up as a gap between
releases -- the same proportional heating cut applied to a leakier (raw) baseline
produces a larger kWh reduction.

```{python}
#| label: monthly-kwh-delta-summary

monthly_total_kwh = {
    label: summarize_by_release_month(df, "delta_total") for label, df in MONTHLY_DELTAS.items()
}
monthly_heating_kwh = {
    label: summarize_by_release_month(df, "delta_heating") for label, df in MONTHLY_DELTAS.items()
}
```

```{python}
#| label: kwh-delta-plot-helper


def plot_monthly_kwh_delta(summary: pl.DataFrame, metric_label: str, population_label: str) -> p9.ggplot:
    """Weighted-mean kWh delta by calendar month, one line per release."""
    return (
        p9.ggplot(summary, p9.aes(x="month", y="mean_delta", color="release", group="release"))
        + p9.geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dotted", color="gray")
        + p9.geom_line(size=1)
        + p9.geom_point(size=2.5)
        + p9.scale_color_manual(values=RELEASE_COLORS, breaks=RELEASE_ORDER)
        + p9.scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda breaks: [f"{b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
        + p9.labs(
            x="Month",
            y="Weighted mean delta (kWh)",
            color="Release",
            title=f"{population_label}: kWh change in {metric_label}",
        )
        + theme_switchbox()
        + p9.theme(figure_size=(10.5, 4.5))
    )
```

## Export

The tables below are the scaling factors this notebook exists to produce: one row per
calendar month, three columns of a **multiplicative factor** on whole-home total electric
use (upgrade 01 vs upgrade 00), one column per ResStock release. They come from the same
ratio-of-weighted-sums used in the percent-change charts, rewritten as
`1 + pct_delta / 100`, so `-23` percent becomes `0.77`. Multiply a month's observed load
by the factor to estimate that month after the upgrade. Column names match the
`RELEASES` keys (`raw`, `sb`, `sb_ach_ratio`) so they can be read as `df.sb` /
`df["sb_ach_ratio"]` without quoting display labels.

The **combined** table is the one that matches BGE billing data which identifies
electric-heating customers without distinguishing strip heat from heat pumps. ER-only
and existing-HP-only tables are pickled alongside it.

```{python}
#| label: export-monthly-pct-wide

# Display label -> identifier used as a column name in the pickle.
RELEASE_COL = {info["label"]: key for key, info in RELEASES.items()}


def monthly_scale_wide(summary: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """One row per month, one upgrade-01 / upgrade-00 load factor per release."""
    return (
        summary.pivot(on="release", index="month", values="pct_delta")
        .rename(RELEASE_COL)
        .with_columns([(pl.col(c) / 100 + 1).alias(c) for c in RELEASES])
        .select("month", *RELEASES)
        .sort("month")
    )


monthly_scale_total_wide = {
    "er": monthly_scale_wide(monthly_total_pct[LABEL_ER]),
    "hp": monthly_scale_wide(monthly_total_pct[LABEL_HP]),
    "combined": monthly_scale_wide(monthly_total_pct[LABEL_COMBINED]),
}
monthly_scale_total_wide["combined"]
```

```{python}
#| label: export-pickle
import pickle

path_cache = Path("../cache")
path_cache.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
path_pkl = path_cache / "rs_release_comp_monthly_pct_total.pkl"
path_pkl.write_bytes(
    pickle.dumps(
        {
            "metric": "scale_factor_total_electric_upg01_vs_upg00",
            "unit": "multiplier",
            "populations": {
                key: df.to_pandas() for key, df in monthly_scale_total_wide.items()
            },
        }
    )
)
print(f"Wrote {path_pkl}")
```

## Closing summary

How much does the ACH-ratio correction change the picture for the ER population, and is
that change concentrated in particular months? We compare the ACH-ratio-corrected release
against raw NREL, month by month across the year, as a percent difference in the
weighted-mean total delta.

```{python}
#| label: closing-divergence

_pivot = monthly_total_summary_er.pivot(on="release", index="month", values="mean_delta").sort("month")
divergence = _pivot.with_columns(
    (
        (pl.col("ACH-ratio corrected") - pl.col("Raw NREL")).abs() / pl.col("Raw NREL").abs() * 100
    ).alias("pct_diff_vs_raw")
).sort("pct_diff_vs_raw", descending=True)
divergence
```

```{python}
#| label: closing-print

annual_raw = annual_total_summary_er.filter(pl.col("release") == "Raw NREL")["mean_delta"][0]
annual_ach = annual_total_summary_er.filter(pl.col("release") == "ACH-ratio corrected")["mean_delta"][0]
winter_raw = winter_total_summary_er.filter(pl.col("release") == "Raw NREL")["mean_delta"][0]
winter_ach = winter_total_summary_er.filter(pl.col("release") == "ACH-ratio corrected")["mean_delta"][0]
worst_month = divergence["month"][0]
worst_pct = divergence["pct_diff_vs_raw"][0]
best_month = divergence["month"][-1]
best_pct = divergence["pct_diff_vs_raw"][-1]

print(f"Annual total-electric savings, weighted mean: {annual_raw:,.0f} kWh (raw) -> {annual_ach:,.0f} kWh (ACH-ratio corrected)")
print(f"  ({(annual_ach - annual_raw) / abs(annual_raw) * 100:+.0f}% change in magnitude)\n")
print(f"Whole-winter total-electric savings, weighted mean: {winter_raw:,.0f} kWh (raw) -> {winter_ach:,.0f} kWh (ACH-ratio corrected)")
print(f"  ({(winter_ach - winter_raw) / abs(winter_raw) * 100:+.0f}% change in magnitude)\n")
print("Month-to-month divergence between raw and ACH-ratio corrected, full year:")
print(f"  {best_pct:.0f}% ({best_month}) to {worst_pct:.0f}% ({worst_month})")

_winter_div = divergence.filter(pl.col("month").is_in(WINTER_MONTH_LABELS)).sort("pct_diff_vs_raw")
print("\nRestricted to the six winter months, where nearly all the kWh sit:")
print(
    f"  {_winter_div['pct_diff_vs_raw'][0]:.0f}% ({_winter_div['month'][0]})"
    f" to {_winter_div['pct_diff_vs_raw'][-1]:.0f}% ({_winter_div['month'][-1]})"
)
```
